blocks.heading: Types of union
blocks.text: Union types classify the basis of membership. A craft union represents a particular skilled occupation; a general union draws workers from a variety of occupations or industries; an industrial union represents different kinds of workers within one industry; a white-collar union represents non-manual office, administrative or professional workers. The distinction concerns who is represented rather than whether the union is effective. A skilled electrician can work in several industries, while one industry can employ skilled tradespeople, drivers, office staff and other workers. Look for the membership rule in a situation rather than inferring the type from the name of a workplace.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A fictional union admits electricians across different industries, while another admits all types of worker in food manufacturing. The first uses a craft basis, the second an industrial basis. A workplace’s industry does not make every union serving it an industrial union.

blocks.heading: Craft union
blocks.text: A craft union is a trade union which represents a particular type of skilled worker. The membership link is the occupation or skill, which can be used in different industries. It can concentrate on the conditions and interests of that trade. This differs from an industrial union covering different occupations within one industry.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A fictional union represents qualified carpenters working in several types of enterprise. The shared craft, rather than one industry, defines its membership.

blocks.heading: General union
blocks.text: A general union is a trade union which represents workers, often unskilled but also semi-skilled, from a variety of trades. Its coverage is broad rather than restricted to one skilled craft or one industry. Members may gain a wide collective voice, though their differing workplaces can create varied priorities.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A fictional union admits cleaners, warehouse workers and other workers across different industries. The broad membership fits a general union, rather than a union limited to one craft.

blocks.heading: Industrial union
blocks.text: An industrial union is a trade union which represents all types of workers in a particular industry. Membership is linked by industry, not one skill; technical, manual and office roles can share that industrial link. It can coordinate industry concerns, though members’ occupations and needs still differ.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A fictional union represents drivers, machine operators and administrative staff in food processing. Different occupations within the stated industry fit an industrial union. A union for one skilled occupation across industries would be craft based.

blocks.heading: White-collar union
blocks.text: A white-collar union represents non-manual workers such as office, administrative or professional staff. Its membership basis concerns the type of occupation rather than simply the colour of clothing or whether an employer uses computers. These workers may share issues of pay, professional responsibility or office conditions.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: A fictional union represents administrative and clerical staff. Its non-manual occupational coverage illustrates the white-collar category; it should not be classified as a craft union merely because some jobs require skill.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain the union types: a fictional union admits welders across several industries; another admits different occupations within the fishing industry.

The welders’ common skilled occupation identifies a craft union. The shared industry, despite different occupations, identifies an industrial union. Classify the membership basis rather than treating all skilled workers as belonging to an industrial union.
